canonicalExplanation.summary: Java objects live on the **heap**. The garbage collector (GC) keeps any object that is **reachable**: connected by a chain of references from a **root** such as a local variable in a running method, a **static field**, or an active thread. Anything unreachable **may** be reclaimed later, at a time the GC chooses. So Java can still **leak memory**: if a long-lived root (a static map, a listener list, a cache) keeps referencing objects you no longer need, they stay reachable forever. The fix is to **remove the reference path**: evict entries, bound the cache, unregister listeners. Calling `System.gc()` doesn't help, because it can't collect anything that is still reachable.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's web service stores every request in `static Map<String, Request> CACHE` "for speed". Memory climbs for days until the service crashes with OutOfMemoryError. Adding System.gc() calls changes nothing. A static cache retains every request object through a map, so bounded eviction removes the unwanted root path rather than forcing a collection. In this lesson you'll diagnose a retention or aliasing problem using a reachability model.

examples.title: A static cache that never forgets
examples.situation: A static cache retains every request object through a map, so bounded eviction removes the unwanted root path rather than forcing a collection.
walkthrough: **A static cache retains every request object through a map:** LEAKY holds all 10 requests.
**So bounded eviction removes the unwanted root path:** BOUNDED drops the eldest entry once it has more than 3.
**Rather than forcing a collection:** we check memory stays flat without any System.gc() call.
examples.result: Memory use is bounded, however long the service runs.

examples.title: The listener that kept screens alive
examples.situation: Closed screens stay in memory because each registered a listener with a long-lived event bus and never unregistered.
walkthrough: The bus (long-lived) references each listener, which references its screen.
Unregister the listener when the screen closes.
The screen becomes unreachable and can be collected.
examples.result: Closed screens no longer accumulate in memory.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Java cannot leak memory because garbage collection frees every object that the application no longer intends to use.
misconceptions.correction: The GC frees only unreachable objects. Anything still referenced from a root, even by mistake, is kept.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why couldn't the GC reclaim the object?

analogy.example: The heap is like **a city of balloons tied by strings**. Some strings are held by people standing on the ground (roots). Any balloon connected by strings to someone on the ground stays; balloons with no connected string **float away** (collected) eventually. A static cache is **a person who never lets go of anything**. Shouting "float away!" (System.gc()) doesn't help while they're still holding the string.
usefulFor: remembering strings to people on the ground
limitations: Balloons float away when the GC decides, not instantly.
Aliases are two strings to the same balloon.

steps.explanation: A static cache retains every request object through a map.
Bounded eviction removes the unwanted root path for older requests.
Only objects with no remaining path can be reclaimed, so we remove LEAKY too.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing reachability. Step 1, Retain: LEAKY size is 10; reachable is all 10. A static cache retains every request object through a map. Step 2, Evict: BOUNDED size is 3; kept is r7, r8, r9. Bounded eviction removes the unwanted root path for older requests. Step 3, Collect: r0..r6 via BOUNDED is removed; still held by is LEAKY. Only objects with no remaining path can be reclaimed, so we remove LEAKY too.

nearTransfer.prompt: Draw the reference chain from a root to an object in three small programs (local variable, static field, list inside a static field). Then remove one link in each and say which objects become unreachable.

farTransfer.prompt: Given a program that runs out of memory, find the retention path (a static list of listeners holding sessions), fix it by unregistering and bounding, and show memory staying flat over 100,000 iterations with Runtime.totalMemory() - freeMemory().

remediation.explanation: When memory grows, ask: **what root still reaches these objects, and through which references?** Break that path (evict, clear, unregister), don't force GC.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The listener that kept screens alive".

recap.summary: To diagnose a retention or aliasing problem using a reachability model, trace reference chains from roots like static fields, locals and threads, remember the GC keeps anything reachable and reclaims the rest later, and fix leaks by removing the unwanted path through eviction, clearing or unregistering.
